summary: IS-IS floods link state information within an area or a domain, but some uses need other scopes. This document defines new PDUs that provide additional flooding scopes and extra space for information.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a message is for one street, sometimes the whole city, but this RFC adds in-between choices. It lets routers share news with just the right-sized group.

questions: what is an is-is flooding scope lsp
what is an fs-lsp in is-is
what is circuit scope flooding in is-is
subtitle: New IS-IS packets that flood link state data to scopes beyond an area or the Level 2 subdomain, with room for far more of it.

tldr.problem: IS-IS can only flood information within an area (Level 1) or the Level 2 subdomain. Some uses need other scopes, such as a single circuit, and a router is limited to 256 LSPs per level.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three new PDUs (FS-LSP, FS-CSNP and FS-PSNP) that carry a Scope field, reuse the existing Update Process, and can use extended TLVs with 16-bit Type and Length fields.
tldr.outcome: Routers gain circuit, level and domain flooding scopes and up to 64 K additional LSPs per level, but the new PDUs are not backwards compatible and every router in a scope must support them.

today: RFC 7356 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. RFC 7357 uses its Extended Level 1 Circuit Scope PDUs for TRILL ESADI.

sections.title: Why New Flooding Scopes
sections.content:
IS-IS routers share link state information by flooding it through the Update Process. Today there are only two scopes: Level 1 LSPs reach all routers in an area, and Level 2 LSPs reach all routers in the Level 2 subdomain. The RFC observes that the same machinery works for any subset of routers, as long as that subset is not partitioned.

Three needs drive the design. First, circuit scope flooding: for example, Appointed Forwarder information from RFC 7176 must reach all RBridges on a broadcast circuit reliably, but IS-IS Hellos are unreliable. Second, RFC 5311 notes that a system can originate at most 256 LSPs per level, and the new PDUs allow a less constraining fix. Third, standard TLVs have an 8-bit length, so information about one object over 255 octets must be split.

Because the PDU Type field is 5 bits (at most 32 types), the new PDUs let many scopes share one PDU type.
sections.plainLanguage: The old system only had two announcement sizes, and some news did not fit either one. The new design adds more sizes without needing a whole new set of rules.

sections.title: Extended TLVs
sections.content:
Standard IS-IS TLVs and sub-TLVs use an 8-bit Type and an 8-bit Length, so one TLV holds at most 255 octets. The RFC adds extended TLVs and extended sub-TLVs that use a 16-bit Type and a 16-bit Length, encoded in network byte order.

  • They are allowed only in Flooding Scope PDUs whose scope is designated for them.
  • A given scope uses either standard or extended TLVs, never both.
  • Extended TLVs and extended sub-TLVs MUST be used together; mixing the two forms is invalid.
  • They do not change the maximum PDU size.

Standard code points MAY be reused: the 8-bit type becomes a 16-bit integer whose top 8 bits are 0, and the length MAY exceed 255.
sections.plainLanguage: A standard label can only describe a short note, like a sticky note. Extended labels are like a bigger notepad, so a long story fits in one piece.

sections.title: The Three New PDUs
sections.content:
The RFC defines FS-LSP (PDU type 10), FS-CSNP (type 11) and FS-PSNP (type 12). Their headers are kept as close as possible to the standard LSP, CSNP and PSNP so that implementations can reuse existing processing logic. The Maximum Area Addresses field is replaced by a Scope field, so the area address checks are not done on these PDUs.

Scope uses bits 1 to 7. Value 0 is reserved and PDUs with it are ignored. Scopes 1 to 63 go with standard TLVs; scopes 64 to 127 go with extended TLVs. In an FS-LSP, bit 8 is the P priority bit; in an FS-PSNP it is the U bit, meaning the scope is unsupported.

An FS-LSP also has Remaining Lifetime, a sequence number, a checksum and an LSPDBOL bit for FS-LSP database overload. The FS LSP ID comes in a Standard format (source ID, pseudonode ID, 1-octet FS LSP number) or an Extended format (source ID plus a 2-octet Extended FS LSP number), chosen per scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The new messages look almost like the old ones, with one extra box that says which group the message is for. That way the same mail-handling steps still work.

sections.title: Update Process Operation
sections.content:
Each supported scope gets its own link state database (FS-LSDB) and its own instance of the Update Process, which follows the IS-IS specification. FS-LSPs, FS-CSNPs and FS-PSNPs are sent only on circuits that take part in that scope, and all routers on a circuit must support a consistent set of scopes.

On a point-to-point circuit, when an adjacency reaches the UP state, FS-CSNPs for all supported scopes MUST be sent and the SRM bit set for the relevant FS-LSPs. An FS-PSNP with U = 1 tells the sender the neighbor does not support that scope, and the SRM bit is then cleared for FS-LSPs of that scope.

On a broadcast circuit, FS PDUs use the same destination addresses as standard PDUs. The DIS generates periodic scope-specific FS-CSNPs, but no scope-specific DIS is elected. A scope that is not level specific makes the DIS of each level send FS PDUs independently, which may cause redundant flooding.

Authentication TLVs MAY be included, with the scope used first to pick the authentication configuration. Setting the P bit asks that an FS-LSP SHOULD be flooded at higher priority, and the bit's original state MUST be kept when the LSP is purged.
sections.plainLanguage: Every group gets its own list of announcements and its own way of checking nothing was missed. Routers only trade lists with neighbors who are in the same group.

sections.title: The Defined Scopes
sections.content:
The RFC defines three families of scope, each with a standard and an extended variant.

  • Circuit scope (L1CS, L2CS, E-L1CS, E-L2CS): contents are specific to the circuit they are flooded on, and a received FS-LSP MUST NOT be flooded on any other circuit. The Extended FS LSP ID format is used. Which TLVs appear is left to each use case.
  • Level flooding scope (L1FS, L2FS, E-L1FS, E-L2FS): extra LSP space for one system. L1 variants flood on all L1 circuits and L2 variants on all L2 circuits. The extended ID format gives 64 K more LSPs per level. The standard LSP #0 from the same IS must be present for the set to be usable, transit information must not be used when LSP #0 has the Overload bit set, and TLVs restricted to LSP #0 must not appear.
  • Domain scope (DFS, E-DFS): the unchanged PDU is flooded on all circuits regardless of level, keeping the originator's identity. For IPv4 or IPv6 routing, FS-LSP #0 with domain scope MUST include TLV 134 or TLV 140. Domain scope for Layer 2 is left undefined until multi-area support exists.
sections.plainLanguage: There are announcements for one hallway, for one floor, and for the whole school. Each one also comes in a plain version and a big-notepad version.

sections.title: Deployment and Scope Announcement
sections.content:
New PDU types are incompatible with legacy implementations, which will likely treat an FS PDU as an error. Flooding is only reliable when all routers in the flooding domain support both FS PDUs and the specific scope. Routers SHOULD send a PSNP with U = 1 when they receive an FS-LSP of an unsupported scope, and SHOULD raise management notifications for such events.

Routers MAY announce supported scopes in IIH PDUs with the Scope Flooding Support TLV (type 243, length 1 to 127), a list of 7-bit scope values. Level 1 LAN IIHs must not advertise L2 scopes, and Level 2 LAN IIHs must not advertise L1 scopes. This TLV MUST NOT affect adjacency formation.

The RFC also covers graceful restart (all FS-LSDBs must synchronize, and a PSNP with U = 1 counts as complete for that scope) and multi-instance use of Instance Identifier TLVs as in RFC 6822.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in a group has to know the new rules, or messages get lost. Routers can wear a name tag listing which groups they belong to.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA records the three PDU types (10, 11, 12), creates the "LSP Flooding Scope Identifier Registry" with Expert Review (values 1 to 127), and registers TLV 243. The scope values defined here run from 1 to 5 for standard TLVs and 64 to 68 for extended TLVs. The TLV codepoint registry is extended to allow values up to 65535, and codepoints above 255 can only be used in PDUs designated for extended TLVs.

On security, the new PDUs face the same issues as standard LSPs, CSNPs and PSNPs. Because they add load on routers, they also add opportunity for denial-of-service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of group numbers so nobody reuses one by accident. The new messages are as safe as the old ones, but more messages means more chances for someone to flood a router.

data.title: FS-LSP fixed header (sizes in octets, ID Length is set by IS-IS)

fields.name: Length Indicator
fields.desc: Length of the fixed header in octets.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Transmitted as zero, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: P and Scope
fields.desc: Priority bit plus a 7-bit flooding scope.

fields.name: PDU Length
fields.desc: Entire PDU length in octets, including the header.

fields.name: Remaining Lifetime
fields.desc: Seconds before the FS-LSP is considered expired.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Sequence number of this FS-LSP (follows the FS LSP ID).

fields.name: Reserved, LSPDBOL, IS Type
fields.desc: FS-LSP database overload bit and IS type.
